# B. Rich OECD countries with the design given {#oecd}

Section {{< var p.sec_oecd >}} of the paper calibrates the model without informal households to the U.S. and France
and changes the U.S. calibration one characteristic at a time: its pension design, its demography, and the
income distribution, voting patterns and taste for leisure that set France apart. Appendix {{< var p.app_US >}} gives
the data and the household heterogeneity of the two. This part shows the calibrations of the U.S., the UK and France
across the IES, the U.S. counterfactuals across the Frisch elasticity and the tax rate against inherited savings, what
changes when the taste for leisure is identified group by group, the U.S. with Medicare among the transfers to the old,
and the UK's calibration, which the deep test of [C6](esc-countries.qmd) uses.

- [B1. Calibration](oecd-ies.qmd): the three calibrations at every IES of the grid.
- [B2. Other parameters](oecd-parameters.qmd): the U.S. counterfactuals across the intertemporal and the Frisch
  elasticity, and the tax rate against inherited savings.
- [B3. Identification of X](oecd-leisure.qmd): the common taste for leisure against one per income group.
- [B4. Medicare among the transfers to the old](oecd-medicare.qmd): the U.S. calibrated with Medicare in the tax
  rate and as a flat benefit, and its counterfactuals.
- [B5. The UK](oecd-uk.qmd): the three calibrations side by side and the UK's income groups.
